rows.title: Financial Accounting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) to properly record transactions in the accounting records of a for-profit business in a manner satisfying ethical and legal requirements.
Analyze the data in the general journal and the general ledger accounts to generate the four required financial statements.
Distinguish and validate the content, form, and purpose of the four required financial statements and how they satisfy the information needs of the users of the financial statements.
Quantify the value of the general accounts in accordance with GAAP.

rows.title: Juvenile Procedures
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Examine the theories of the causes and social consequences of juvenile delinquency.
Analyze the structure, role, and function of juvenile justice.
Analyze judicial decisions which extended constitutional protections to juveniles.
Evaluate theories and concepts of delinquency, prevention, treatment, and control.
Evaluate and explain historical and contemporary data relating to juvenile delinquency rates and their intersection with demographic variables.

rows.title: Administration of Justice and the LGBTQ+ Community
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the difference between sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression.
Describe effective strategies for building trust and relationships between the LGBTQ+ community and the justice system.
Describe how to create an inclusive workplace in the justice system for LGBTQ+ employees.
Identify effective responses to hate crimes and domestic violence by the criminal justice system in the LGBTQ+ community.

rows.title: Fingerprints
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Select appropriate sequential fingerprint development techniques for porous and non-porous surfaces.
Interpret and classify fingerprint patterns using the Henry system, the National Crime Information Center system, and the Integrated Automated Fingerprint Identification System.
Identify causes of error in fingerprint comparisons.
Anticipate and address legal and scientific challenges to fingerprint identification.

rows.title: Terrorism and Counterterrorism
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Differentiate terrorism from criminal or military violence by using a value-free definition that focuses on the victims and public safety.
Integrate an understanding of terrorist historical and political motivations with techniques used in terrorism and counterterrorism.
Appraise major terrorist organizations, their tactics, and strategies.
Evaluate strategies for protecting public safety through preparedness, prevention, mitigation, and investigation.
Distinguish the particular challenges democracies face in dealing with the threat of terrorism.

rows.title: Student Campus Patrol Work Experience
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply the practical and typical duties of a Student Campus Police Officer as assigned while working under direct or indirect supervision.
Apply the theory, techniques, and knowledge gained in the law enforcement curriculum in a positive manner.
Engage in assigned duties without bias, prejudice, or personal feeling.
Utilize radio communications and police equipment in a proper and safe manner.
Exhibit professional behavior as it relates to the law enforcement code of ethics.

rows.title: Criminal Justice Career Preparation
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe educational resources related to employment in the San Francisco Police Department or other law enforcement agencies.
Create a portfolio to assist in successfully completing the entry level Q2 Police Officer examination process for the San Francisco Police Department or other law enforcement agencies.
Identify testing qualities that law enforcement agencies look for in potential candidates.
Describe the main components of the application process for the San Francisco Police Department or other law enforcement agencies.

rows.title: The Origins and History of Race Theory and Modern Racism
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Distinguish between race, ethnicity, nationality, caste, and socio-economic class.
Analyze race and racism as socially constructed.
Analyze the evolution of ideas about race/color and their connection to cultural ideas and practices.
Compare and assess ideas about race/color and culture between different contemporary societies and between different historical periods.
Trace how race theory and racism have been insinuated into the practical worlds of politics, economics, social structures, intellectual discourse, and popular culture.
Analyze 20th-century challenges to racism in the U.S.

rows.title: American Sign Language Part II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and use American Sign Language with intermediate elementary linguistic structures appropriately in a variety of language functions.
Explain general historical factors and contexts that have contributed to American Deaf culture and the development of American Sign Language.
Examine culturally appropriate behavior with Deaf people in various social situations.

rows.title: Philippine Culture and Society
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the impact of colonialism on regional and local cultural development on coastal, lowland, and upland populations.
Analyze the role of language in the development of Philippine culture.
Compare the various belief systems that exist and thrive in Philippine society.
Analyze the various kinship strategies employed in Philippine society and Filipino communities abroad.

rows.title: Culture, Gender and Sexuality
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply the general perspective, terminology, and theories of cultural anthropology to the study of gender and contemporary gender issues
Describe and explain sexual and gender diversity in non-Western cultures
Compare gender practices of diverse cultures
Explain the complex relationship between human culture and human biology as applied to gender

rows.title: Anthropology of Cannabis
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the diversity of cannabis cultures using the four sub-disciplines of anthropology.
Identify anthropological theories, methodologies, and techniques for studying to cannabis and hemp.
Analyze forms of cannabis consumption across cultures and lifestyles.
Apply anthropological research concepts to understanding the cultivation, distribution, and medicinal practices of cannabis and hemp.
Compare contemporary and historical cannabis and hemp consumption practices across societies.

rows.title: Architecture Design Studio II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Create architectural solutions to a set of project requirements.
Evaluate a proposed architectural solution against social, cultural, and project requirements.
Analyze and communicate the design contexts and processes visually, orally, in writing, and through physical and digital models.
Communicate using 2D and 3D architectural language that responds to site, program, materials, and structure.
Differentiate how architects create an iterative design process.

rows.title: Professional Practice
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Compare the roles and responsibilities of the different participants in the design and construction process.
Analyze the design and building process from concept to completion in relation to social, environmental, and regulatory issues.
Compare the differing methods of project delivery, the corresponding forms of service contracts, and the types of documentation required to render competent and responsible service.
Describe and differentiate amongst the licensing and training requirements for architects, interior designers, engineers, construction managers, and building contractors.
Assess basic business principles as they apply to professional practice in architecture and related fields.

rows.title: Delineation and Rendering
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Produce fundamental and related architectural drawings; choosing appropriate types that are relevant and credible.
Create representations of architectural ideas and concepts.
Choose from a palette of colors to best represent and communicate qualities of architectural forms and space using various color media and techniques.
Arrange a series of drawn representations into a visual composition that communicates major design intentions into a visual and multi-layered formal presentation.
Appraise the efficacy of an architectural graphic presentation against the design intentions.

rows.title: History of Architecture I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Compare significant features, characteristics and representative buildings of various architectural movements completed before 1400 C.E. using accurate terminology and interpreted through visual environmental literacy.
Evaluate how cultural, climatic, ecological, technological, socioeconomic, and public health conditions have impacted the design of the built environment before 1400 C.E.
Analyze the ways architecture before 1400 C.E. has served diverse human needs, values, and aspirations.

rows.title: Latin American Art History
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ historical and visual literacy methods in order to analyze Latin American art and architecture.
Distinguish various Latin American art movements and their social contexts since colonization.
Evaluate the heritage of Latin American art as both distinct from and connected to European art.
Identify Amerindian and African-inspired thematic and stylistic elements expressed in Latin American art and their diaspora.

rows.title: History of Comic and Sequential Art
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the variety of techniques and formal visual elements of comic and sequential art.
Define the various styles of comic and sequential artists to analyze their components and characteristics.
Describe the emergence, development, and subsequent history of comic and sequential art with reference to historical and social factors.
Relate works of comic and sequential art to the historical, cultural and sociological contexts in which they were created.
Compare stylistic elements that distinguish aesthetic and cultural trends of pivotal works by major comic and sequential artists from the medieval period to the present.

rows.title: Renaissance Art
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify formal visual elements of style.
Analyze works of Renaissance art using art-historical terminology.
Compare the contributions of individual artists to the development of Renaissance art.
Examine Renaissance painting within its cultural context.

rows.title: Color
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify color attributes (hue, value, chroma), comprehend their organization in various color models throughout time and explore processes for manipulating color in own designs for effective visual communication.
Recognize individual artist palettes in relation to different eras, cultures, resources and media, and the origins and unique properties of pigments.
Distinguish color harmonies and contrasts and successfully employ them for effective visual communication in own designs.
Analyze and evaluate color interactions in art and design in a range of media, and communicate observations by engaging in critical discourse using appropriate terminology.
Research, evaluate and discuss perceptual, psychological, organizational, cultural, symbolic and expressive aspects of color use in fine art and design and color influence in human experience.

rows.title: Intermediate Figure Drawing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply intermediate-level knowledge of drawing techniques to create drawings with nuanced value transitions and proportions, using both monochromatic and color media.
Apply an intermediate-level understanding of major muscle groups and bone structures to figure drawing.
Analyze figurative art developments across diverse cultures, synthesizing nuanced historical and contemporary artistic trends.
Analyze one's own work and the work of peers using intermediate-level critical thinking skills.

rows.title: Intermediate Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ intermediate painting techniques to the construction of paintings in several styles and genres.
Compose original paintings to convey ideas and feelings.
Apply knowledge of historical and contemporary painting trends towards a deeper understanding of how and what to paint.
Analyze paintings employing the language and methods of critique.

rows.title: Beginning Intaglio & Relief Printmaking
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify intaglio and relief prints of diverse cultures with an understanding of the historical, cultural, and socio-political context of the techniques and artistic content employed.
Use basic intaglio and relief plate making techniques to develop imagery with regard to a historical, cultural and/or contemporary issue and make image improvements.
Use basic intaglio and relief inking and printing techniques to support plate image content and print small editions.
Apply design principles and printmaking terminology in analyzing and discussing prints with regard to content and individual expression.
Practice safe working methods when using equipment, tools, and supplies.

rows.title: Beginning Sculpture
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply three-dimensional design principles and terminology toward analyzing and discussing sculptural forms in both written and verbal methods.
Identify essential categories of historical and contemporary sculpture.
Evaluate and solve problems during the creation of a work of art in three-dimensions.
Employ additive and reductive working processes using traditional and non-traditional materials to reflect idea development.
Establish safe working methods and employ good craftsmanship in the creation of sculpture.

rows.title: Survey of Art from the Renaissance to Contemporary
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from the Renaissance to the contemporary period employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture and critique them in terms of aesthetic, sociopolitical, religious, historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from the Renaissance to the contemporary period.

rows.title: Community Issues & Leadership
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze community concerns faced by Asian Americans, including current and structural issues.

Analyze models of critical leadership and intersectional identities, examining intersectional identities of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, sovereignty, language, and/or age in Asian American communities.

Analyze methods and examples of effective leadership within Asian American communities, organizations, and movements, describing and actively engaging in anti-racist and anti-colonial issues and practices and movements for a just and equitable society.

Interpret key public policies and how these policies impact today's Asian American communities, including an Ethnic Studies analysis, utilzing frameworks, theories and knowledge produced by Asian Americans.

Assess Asian American communities, leaders, organizations, and movements by articulating critical Asian American Studies concepts of race, racism, self-determination and liberation, through the lens of anti-colonialism, anti-racism, and equity.

rows.title: Asian American Women
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze events, economic and political forces, and social movements that have influenced the experiences of Asian women in the United States, using key Ethnic Studies concepts.

Exhibit an understanding of the differences and similarities of migration histories of women from Asia to the United States through literature, critically analyzing how issues of migration influence Asian American women's lives.

Evaluate critically how Asian American women have acted in response to their experiences in the United States by applying the theories and methodologies of Ethnic Studies, Asian American Studies, Social and Behavioral Sciences, including theory and knowledge produced by Asian American feminist scholars to describe the critical events, histories, cultures, intellectual traditions, contributions, creative expressions, lived-experiences and social struggles of Asian American women, with a particular emphasis on agency and group-affirmation.

Analyze how Asian American women have used creative expression and the humanities to explore the intersection of race and racism as they relate to gender, sexuality, class, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, sovereignty, language, and/or age.

Review critically how Asian American women have experienced and enacted struggle, resistance, solidarity, liberation, racial, gender and social justice, pursuing historic, current, and structural issues, in communal, national, international and transnational politics.

Describe and apply key theoretical concepts from feminist of color writing, including oppression, systems of power and approaches to social change to the experience of Asian American women, and comparing the experience of Asian American women with the experiences of other BIPOC women in the United States.

rows.title: Asian American Community Field Study
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the history and function of at least one Asian American community based organization.
Apply standards of professional conduct in the community workplace.
Perform workplace tasks appropriate for Asian American community organizations.

rows.title: Asian Societies and Cultures through Film
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Interpret religious and cultural traditions in East Asia, India, and Southeast Asia as illustrated in film.
Describe and contextualize socio-cultural issues as represented in East Asian, Indian, and Southeast Asian films.
Distinguish ethnic and cultural differences in Asian societies as portrayed in film.
Analyze depictions of colonization, independence movements, and communism in East Asia, India and Southeast Asia using film.

rows.title: Planets
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain basic terminology of introductory planetary science.
Evaluate claims and information concerning the planets for plausibility, using the scientific methods of inquiry, logic and reasoning.
Analyze the manifestation of physical laws in the realm of planetary sciences that are operating in students' lives.
Conclude that planetary information is revealed through observations, experiments and modeling, integrating the knowledge into a cosmic perspective of planets' places in the universe.
Compare the evolution, structure, and properties of the solar system's planets to other planetary systems.
Appraise how knowledge gained from planetary sciences has affected humanity's concept of the natural world and our global society.

rows.title: Reflashing and Factory Scan Tools for Technicians
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and describe the hardware, software, and networking components of modern and next generation automobiles.
Operate the correct hardware and software needed to reflash automobiles.
Set up the correct environment for reflashing an automobile.
Apply appropriate safety procedures while handling automotive technology.

rows.title: Introduction to Auto Painting and Refinishing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe and employ shop safety practices related to auto body repair and painting involving urethane, polyurethane, and water-based refinishing.
Describe the design, maintenance, and use of different automotive painting tools and equipment utilized when applying refinishing materials to a panel or test piece.
Prepare and apply paint to an automotive panel.
Apply various techniques for removing minor paint imperfections on automobiles and maintaining refinished surfaces.

rows.title: Custom Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe proper safety procedures for the use and handling of automotive paint and related products.
Apply proper application of surface preparation products and primers.
Create and apply graphic designs using masking and air brush techniques
Prepare mid-coat and clear-coat type products within local Volatile Organic Compounds (VOC) guidelines and regulations.
Integrate color sanding and polish finishing techniques to acceptable industry standards.

rows.title: Brakes, Suspension, Alignment
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assess brake and suspension systems, parts, operation, and nomenclature.
Evaluate and repair of power brake and anti-lock brake systems.
Diagnose and repair suspension and steering systems.
Evaluate and adjust vehicle wheel alignment settings.

rows.title: Introduction to Hybrid and EV Auto Maintenance and Repair
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain introductory principles of motor and generator basics, and battery basics
Demonstrate safety procedures and describe their critical importance
Perform routine maintenance per manufacturer specifications
Diagnose and solve mechanical and electrical problems
Describe the locations and functions of hybrid system components in a vehicle

rows.title: Custom Metal Fabrication
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ all shop safety practices related to metal fabrication of metal parts.
Set up and operate various metal shaping and welding equipment per industry safety standards.
Measure and cut raw metal into appropriate patterns and form and shape them into metal parts.
Apply appropriate metal finishing techniques using files, grinders, sanders, shapers, hammers, and dollies.

rows.title: Mass Media and Society
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize the history, organization, and functions of various mass media.
Evaluate the fundamentals of historical and contemporary media/communications methods of analysis.
Compare the roles and effects of various media on the individual and society.
Describe the economics, business models, and motivations of corporate media.
Analyze the influence and impact of digital media and the Internet on traditional media industries.

rows.title: Audio Production
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the basic physics of sound and acoustics.
Describe the theory and application of the components of analog and digital audio equipment.
Apply basic techniques of sound production using appropriate digital audio recorders and common audio software programs and plugins.
Compare the technical and aesthetic aspects of sound for a variety of audio careers.

rows.title: Music Mixing Studio
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Diagram the path of signal flow through a large format console, patch bay, and associated components.
Prepare and mix a multi-track session into a stereo mix using equalization, dynamics, and time-based processing at an intermediate level.
Analyze and discuss the aesthetics in the mixes and mastering of different recordings and styles of music.
Display professionalism and effective application of workforce protocol in communication and behavior in the music mixing studio.

rows.title: Audio for the Web/Podcasting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Produce and distribute audio content for the web.
Create audio content that tells a story.
Use current technology to promote audio content to target audience.
Analyze the differences between audio broadcasting and podcasting.

rows.title: Video Editing Premiere Pro - Introduction
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and apply the basic techniques and aesthetics of video editing using Adobe Premiere Pro editing software
Organize and complete a digital video editing project with common video editing techniques and aesthetics using Adobe Premiere Pro software
Analyze and apply digital video effects, titles, and object movement to video editing projects at an introductory level
Analyze and apply appropriate video compression options for creating and exporting video projects at an introductory level

rows.title: Intermediate Studio Video Production
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate studio production processes, roles, and related TV technology.
Plan, produce, and analyze program segments for production requirements and quality.
Operate studio and control room equipment effectively.
Collaborate as a video production team member utilizing in-person, online communication and industry terminology in a professional manner.

rows.title: Industry Internship
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Perform essential tasks appropriate for the media industry environment
Formulate reasonable and measurable occupational learning objectives
Analyze work experiences and their relevance to one's educational and/or occupational goals

rows.title: General Biology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Construct the framework of biology using evolution as a unifying concept.
Synthesize evidence supporting evolution as the mechanism for the diversity of life and distinguish diverse forms of life.
Characterize the relationship of form to function of the major plant phyla and explain how this is related to the evolution of land plants.
Evaluate the interactions between organisms and their environment through ecological principles.
Perform, document and analyze scientific experiments, and apply critical thinking to explain results.

rows.title: Human Physiology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Use the basic terminology and concepts of human physiology to describe the mechanisms of normal physiological processes.
Construct the relationship between different physiological mechanisms necessary to create a working homeostatic regulatory set of mechanisms in the human system.
Apply the concepts and principles of hypothesis testing, using physiological laboratory skills to quantify and compare normal human physiological function and variability.
Construct and communicate an argument for physiological mechanisms using collected laboratory data.

rows.title: Emerging Diseases
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe how epidemiology is used to identify and assess emerging communicable and non-communicable diseases
Give examples how climate change and ecological factors, vaccine hesitancy, and antibiotic resistance are driving new and re-emerging infectious diseases and fungal pathogens.
Examine the role of changes in diet and lifestyle patterns driving a global epidemic of diabetes, obesity, and other non-communicable conditions.
Evaluate the effectiveness of common methods of disease control and prevention.

rows.title: Nutrition and Culinary Arts
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the relationship between dietary choices, nutrient metabolism, and health.
Justify food preparation methodology and meal planning for health.
Use reliable scientific evidence to critique theories of weight management and dietary recommendations.

rows.title: Biology of HIV
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate and communicate basic epidemiological concepts and terminology that relate to disease transmission within populations.
Assess and communicate the efficacy of different HIV prevention, treatment and cure-based approaches within the context of scientific studies and clinical trials.
Evaluate and apply scientific inquiry and investigation of evidence for the origins and emergence of HIV/AIDS.

rows.title: Ecology of the City of San Francisco
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe human impact on the ecology of San Francisco.
Analyze how abiotic factors shape San Francisco's unique natural resources.
Describe some of San Francisco's unique natural resources.
Evaluate conflicting interests in urban open space preservation.

rows.title: Ecology of the San Francisco Bay Delta
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify key drivers and processes that affect the community structure and dynamics of the San Francisco Bay Delta ecosystems.
Understand ecological concepts and apply them to management issues faced within the San Francisco Bay Delta.
Evaluate scientific information and apply it in the field to specific ecological observations.
Observe and identify the diversity of habitats within the San Francisco Bay Delta and their associated fauna and flora.

rows.title: Marine Biology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Recognize the major groups of organisms found in marine ecosystems.
Synthesize knowledge of physical and chemical processes to help describe biological adaptations across a diversity of organisms in the context of these organisms’ various marine habitats.
Evaluate the interactions between organisms and their marine environment through ecological principles.
Describe the physical characteristics of the world's oceans and their basins and regions.

rows.title: The Biology of Cancer
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain how the perception of cancer and theories of its causes have changed throughout history because of important scientific discoveries.
Outline the processes leading to unchecked cell growth and cancer.
Compare the various mechanistic, biological ways by which cancer can occur.
Analyze strategies for preventing and treating cancer.
Evaluate critically both scientific and non-scientific information on causes, treatment, and prevention of cancer.

rows.title: Recombinant DNA Biotechnology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and manipulate DNA and RNA using basic techniques including gel electrophoresis and UV spectroscopy.
Perform advanced techniques of genome analysis including real-time PCR following a detailed protocol.
Describe theoretical concepts of molecular biology and genomics that are needed to work in the biotechnology industry.
Analyze recombinant DNA experiments.
Create an accurate record of lab work and results of experiments.

rows.title: Biotechnology Internship Support
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ career skills to search for potential jobs or internships.
Communicate effectively and appropriately in a biotechnology-related professional setting.
Identify and use computer based tools and resources to investigate internship-related scientific topics.
Describe, articulate, and evaluate methods and scientific concepts related to the research project performed at the internship site.

rows.title: Introductory Stem Cell Internship Support
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Use appropriate industry-standard terminology to summarize and explain the overarching relevance of research being conducted in a research laboratory.
Explain laboratory procedures used in a research laboratory, specifying how these procedures serve the lab’s research objectives.
Identify and use industry-standard computer-based tools and resources to investigate scientific topics and prepare a scientific presentation.
Develop a research paper/project proposal that conforms with the research objectives of a research laboratory.

rows.title: Introduction to PCR
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the theoretical principles of PCR using industry-standard terminology.
Perform standard protocols to execute PCR procedures.
Analyze the results of a PCR experiment.
Describe applications of the PCR technique.

rows.title: Biotechnology Work Experience
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply standards of professional conduct and communication skills in the biotechnology work environment.
Employ the technical skills needed to work in an entry-level position in the biotechnology industry.

rows.title: Structural Building Information Modeling (BIM) in Revit
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Use the interface of Revit Structure effectively.
Generate project datum including project basepoints, grids, levels, and reference planes.
Design and generate 3D structural models and related 2D drawings using Autodesk's Revit Structure.
Create concrete column details to American Concrete Institute (ACI) standards with given engineering data.
Create framed steel connection details to industry standards and American Institute of Steel Construction (AISC) specifications.
Summarize building information modeling (BIM) and the benefits of bidirectional associativity.

rows.title: Advanced AutoCAD Techniques
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Differentiate solids, surfaces, and meshes when creating 3D models
Create a 3D model to render a scene with materials and lighting
Customize the AutoCAD interface to create custom commands

rows.title: Introduction to Wine
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Differentiate between and illustrate American and European laws related to grape growing and winemaking.

outcomes: Interact orally at the novice mid-level with grammatical accuracy and intelligible pronunciation.
Write descriptively in French using accurate grammar and spelling at the novice mid-level.
Explain short written French texts and culture-related materials using structures and vocabulary at the novice mid-level.
Express a cultural awareness of the French-speaking world at the novice mid-level.

rows.title: Grammar Review and Composition
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze complex French sentence structures at the advanced low-level.
Apply editing techniques and strategies to locate and correct errors at the advanced low-level.
Produce written and oral communication using proper French structures, while avoiding literal translation and interference from English.
Interpret complex texts in French identifying main ideas and nuances of meaning using an advanced low-level knowledge of French syntax.

rows.title: Intermediate French
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Express ideas and personal opinions orally using communicative structures in French at an intermediate high-level
Discuss literary and expository texts in French at an intermediate high-level
Produce a cohesive text at a high-intermediate level using the studied structures
Analyze French and francophone cultures through texts, songs, films, and the textbook's cultural notes

rows.title: Contemporary French Culture and Civilization
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the evolution of French art and culture in a historical context from the entre-deux-guerres period to the present.
Summarize France's government and political systems, political parties, and the evolution thereof.
Describe the French educational system.
Explain the importance of the land and language to French identity.
Evaluate current issues affecting French society.

rows.title: GIS Analysis and Modeling
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Locate and utilize GIS data from online resources.
Formulate algorithms for spatial analysis, 3D-modeling, terrain modeling, and data editing.
Identify and implement procedures for data collection using remote sensing or GPS.

rows.title: Cultural Geography
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize the major concepts and traditional approaches to the study of culture and cultural geography.
Appraise the processes and consequences of the globalization of culture and economy in the contemporary world.
Evaluate the origins and distributions of basic cultural geographic phenomena.

rows.title: Physical Geology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply scientific inquiry and investigation of evidence to critically evaluate geologic principles and phenomena.
Use both diagrams and writing to communicate fundamental geologic concepts and principles effectively.
Apply scientific principles, theories, or models to explain the behavior of geologic phenomena at various rates across geologic time.
Evaluate the interrelationship between human activities and geologic processes and the impact of this interrelationship on both society and the physical Earth.

rows.title: Historical Geology Lab
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Investigate historical geology through a variety of scientific inquiry techniques.
Analyze and evaluate historical geology data.
Apply scientific principles, theories, or models to interpret geologic histories and predict future environmental changes.

rows.title: Environmental Geology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize and explain observations of environmental conditions and processes using diagrams and precise written expression.
Analyze geologic hazards and describe strategies to mitigate them.
Evaluate arguments relating to global environmental and resource issues.
Differentiate between natural and human-induced environmental change.
Compare geologic processes related to hazards, resources and climate that take place at different rates and across wide ranges of geologic time.

rows.title: Phlebotomy Technician
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply principles of anatomy, physiology, and medical terminology of the circulatory system to the practice of a phlebotomist.
Apply safe and professional blood collection procedures to patients with a variety of ages and health conditions within the scope of practice of a phlebotomist.
Recognize and correct complications of phlebotomy techniques, and problems with specimen collection, transport and processing.
Analyze the legal and ethical issues encountered by the phlebotomist in the clinical laboratory department.
Communicate with patients, families, and healthcare providers within expectations of the profession.

rows.title: Professional Practice Preparation and Certification
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply knowledge of patient confidentiality, HIPAA regulations, professionalism, and medical ethics in a health care facility.
Adhere to universal precautions as published by the Centers for Disease Control (CDC).

Perform entry-level skills appropriate for the medical assistant, medical administrative assistant, medical receptionist, medical evaluation assistant, or medical clinic assistant in a health care setting.
Apply various techniques for preparing for certification exams.

rows.title: United States Women's History:  1890-Present
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and explain key social, cultural, political, and economic factors influencing the history of women in the United States from 1890 to the present.
Explain the major historical developments in United States women's history from 1890 to the present.
Describe and analyze the impact of race, class, ethnicity, and sexual orientation on the experience and status of women from 1890 to the present.
Analyze, evaluate, and synthesize historical evidence and interpretations in writing, drawing on primary and secondary sources.

rows.title: History of the Mexican American/Chicano
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Interpret Mexican American/Chicano history in the United States by using different historiographic and social science methodologies.
Explain the artistic and cultural history of Mexican Americans/Chicanos in the United States.
Analyze major political and economic trends and events and their significance to the history of Mexican Americans/Chicanos in the United States.
Compare major social and cultural developments, their causes and effects, and their historical significance as relates to the history of Mexican Americans/Chicanos in the United States.
Evaluate the history of Mexican Americans/Chicanos in the United States in a transnational context.

rows.title: African American History From Ancestral West Africa to the Civil War
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Distinguish and interpret the African cultural heritage in the antebellum United States.

Analyze a range of sociocultural, economic, and spiritual contributions that African American people have made to the growth and development of the antebellum United States and the rise of American capitalism.
Compare the African American experience in the United States with other social, indigenous, and ethnic groups of the pre-Civil War (National) Era.
Identify and explain specific African American ideologies and belief systems as they evolved prior to the U.S. Civil War to administer to the special needs of Black people.

Evaluate and synthesize historical evidence and interpretations drawn from both primary and secondary sources as related to African American history within the African diaspora through the United States Civil War.

rows.title: Western Civilization
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze, evaluate, and synthesize historical evidence and interpretations and use methods of inquiry and expression appropriate to the study of Early Western history.
Interpret primary and secondary sources to be integrated as support in a written argument or interpretation.
Evaluate the impact of a wide breadth of trends and changes in politics, society, and economic organization related to Early Western history.
Explain the major technological and scientific developments in Early Western history, their causes and effects, and their historical significance.
Examine artistic and cultural traditions in their historical context in the history of Early West Civilization.

rows.title: United States History to 1877
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to interpret primary and secondary sources and to compose an argument which uses supportive evidence.
Demonstrate an understanding of U.S. History through analytical categories such as race, class, gender, sexuality, ethnicity.
Analyze economic, political, and cultural developments as well as social movements and assess their historical significance.
Analyze the United States prior to 1877 within a global context.
Analyze the relevance of Early American History to the present day.
Examine artistic and cultural traditions in their historical context in the history of the United States until 1877.

rows.title: Disease Process
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the common causes of morbidity, disability, and mortality with emphasis on environmental factors and immune system disease.
Define disease and identify the common diagnostic and therapeutic resources used by health care professionals to diagnose and relate those to applicable diagnostic and procedural coding systems.
Apply an understanding of drug indication, desired effect, contraindications, adverse effects, and classifications to the treatment of disease.
Recognize carcinogenesis and analyze common aspects of malignant and benign neoplasia

Correlate the etiology, signs and symptoms, diagnostic and treatment modalities, and prevention of common diseases and conditions associated with body systems and genetic, developmental, mental health, and metabolic disorders.

rows.title: ICD-10-CM Coding
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Define the code conventions used to locate an ICD-10-CM code in the alphabetic and tabular volumes of the codebook.
Apply the principles of the Uniform Hospital Discharge Data Set (UHDDS) guidelines to the rules of coding, reporting, and sequencing.
Analyze the various medical record documents utilized to code inpatient admissions and outpatient encounters.
Select and assign ICD-10-CM codes to diagnoses and medical reports according to the UHDDS guidelines.
Apply the concepts of physician queries, case audits, and Present on Admission activities.

rows.title: Professional Practice I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe professionalism and ethical behavior in a facility-based health information position.
Explain the expectations of the health information professional and the functions and advantages of electronic health records.
Apply existing health information requirements and standards to the control, use, and release of medical information when processing requests for patients.
Perform technical skills in preparation for the health information field experience.

rows.title: Introduction to Addiction and Recovery Counseling
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the requirements for becoming a Certified Substance Use Disorder (SUD) Counselor and the support resources available.
Assess the role of the SUD counselor in a public health context with attention to the core competencies and attributes required for success.
Examine the complexities of transitioning from a client to a counselor and the role of self-care as a foundation for success.

rows.title: Professional Skills for Community Mental Health Workers
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Perform entry-level community mental health worker skills with professionalism and within ethical boundaries and scope of practice.
Apply peer coaching and counseling skills in individual and group settings.
Assess client risks and de-escalate crisis situations.
Explain and apply trauma-informed practices and client care management.

rows.title: Conflict Resolution Skills in Health
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze causes of conflict in personal and community health.
Examine the role of power and culture in managing conflict in community health settings.
Perform essential communication skills used in conflict management.

rows.title: CHW Principles & Practice 2
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency of the core competencies for providing person-centered assessment, health education, counseling and care management/navigation services.
Assess and demonstrate professional skills including teamwork, professional boundaries, scope of practice, conflict resolution and self care practices.
Analyze and apply key competencies for working at the group and community levels including group facilitation and community diagnosis, organizing and advocacy skills.

rows.title: Health and Social Justice
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Compare a public health model that considers structural, social and economic determinants to an individual lifestyle and behavior change model to explain disparities in prevalent health conditions.
Compare U.S. policy on access to healthcare to other developed nations and analyze emerging U.S. public health and healthcare legislation through an equity lens.
Analyze the contribution of social inequality, economic inequality and environmental conditions to disparate health outcomes.
Analyze how discrimination based on race, socioeconomic status, and gender become embodied in disparate health outcomes.
Analyze advocacy strategies, including public testimony, editorials, community organizing, policy briefs, policy change, and large-scale social movements, that reduce health inequities.
Summarize disparities in health outcomes in the US by race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and gender
Interpret public health epidemiologic data and resources to assess current health disparities.

rows.title: Drugs, Health, and Society
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Distinguish between drug use, misuse, and abuse, including the concepts of tolerance, dependence and the impact of various drug administration methods.

Examine the biological impact of common substances of abuse, including psychotherapeutic effects, the neurological and physiological responses to various types of drugs and the consequences of short- and long-term substance use and abuse.

Apply a public health framework for understanding drug use, including identification of risk and protective factors associated with the use of specific substances based on age, sex, education, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, race and age at first initiation.

Analyze current public health perspectives on substance abuse, considering the broad social, political, economic and cultural factors that influence substance abuse as well as strategies for prevention, education and treatment.

Interpret reliable epidemiologic public health data such as incidence, prevalence, and trends in drug, tobacco and alcohol use, to assess the health impact on communities, specifically low-income communities and communities of color.
Examine and discuss the history of legislative efforts to regulate and control alcohol and drugs, making connections to contemporary drug policy development.
Analyze drug policies and arguments on controversial issues such as the “War on Drugs,” drug testing in the workplace, or legalization/decriminalization of specific drugs.

rows.title: Violence as a Public Health Issue
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the social, political, behavioral, and structural causes of violence.
Use a public health approach to analyze the prevalence and risk factors for various forms of violence.
Parse the impacts of violence and the role of resiliency for individuals and communities.
Examine programs, public policies, and strategies for violence prevention.
Apply civic participation skills for safer and healthier communities.

rows.title: Introduction to Public Health
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Distinguish between personal and public health.
Explain the foundational concepts, major functions, and historical development of public health.
Analyze determinants of health, their role in health inequities, and their relationship to health policy.
Apply epidemiological concepts and methods to the analysis, prevention, and control of disease and injury.
Outline the process of community organizing, community building, and health promotion programming.
Assess and address contemporary public health challenges and how they affect specific populations.
Discuss the organization of public health and healthcare in the United States.
Assess and utilize credible information on public health.

rows.title: Chronic Conditions Management
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Examine the multiple factors that influence the causes and consequences of common chronic health conditions across diverse populations.
Discuss medical, behavioral science and public health approaches for the successful prevention and management of chronic conditions, including team-based care and the role of frontline providers.
Analyze the principles and approaches to patient self-management.
Apply person-centered concepts and skills, including the use of Motivational Interviewing and action planning, for supporting patients in the successful management of chronic conditions.

rows.title: Professional Skills for Addiction and Recovery Counselors
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply the counselor practice dimensions and core functions, including counseling skills, in behavioral health settings.
Analyze the expectations and responsibilities of professional conduct, service delivery, and field placement, including the roles and responsibilities of interns and supervisors.
Apply the principles of professional ethics and client confidentiality.
Demonstrate understanding of the requirements for passing the state AOD credentialing exam through preparation and practice.

rows.title: Interpreting in Healthcare II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply standards, protocols, and skills in managing moderate to complex interpreting encounters.
Describe common medical conditions and examine cultural and linguistic implications.
Exhibit intercultural communication skills in managing diverse interactions and power dynamics.
Employ the six-steps ethical decision-making process to solve ethical dilemmas.
Apply proper skills in using various interpreting modalities.

rows.title: Family Systems
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assess the effectiveness of wellness and recovery best practices and interventions with families in behavioral health settings.
Produce service delivery documentation based on behavioral health standards.
Evaluate the impact of self-awareness when working with families.

rows.title: Elder Abuse Prevention
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the risk factors and indicators of elder abuse, neglect, and exploitation.
Explain legal and ethical duties to report abuse and services available.

rows.title: Transgender Health
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Define key concepts and terminology, and access reliable research and resources, related to transgender and nonbinary communities.
Assess the health status, health needs and health inequities of transgender and nonbinary communities.
Apply trans-inclusive concepts and skills for working with transgender and nonbinary clients and communities.

rows.title: Music, Art, and Literature: Traditional
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify traditional artistic figures before the nineteenth century and basic aesthetic characteristics.
Combine a formal understanding of aesthetics with a personal reaction to the arts to enable an informed response to artistic expression.
Analyze works of art in their historical and cultural contexts through discussion and writing.
Evaluate the influence of non-Western cultures on Western artistic movements as well as the ways in which the idea of a Western canon was constructed.

rows.title: African-American Music, Art and Literature
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify elements of the African and African-American aesthetic in modern American music, sculpture, paintings, architecture, and literature.
Summarize the major contributions of the African-American canon of artistic expression.
Analyze texts by and concerning African-American authors for their cultural and historical context through discussion and writing.
Describe the blending of African and European cultures that creates a unique African-American expression in several artistic genres.

rows.title: Human Sexuality
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate current and historical methodologies used to study human sexuality, including physiological, biological, and anatomical aspects of sexuality, as well as relevant cultural values.
Compare the anatomical, physiological, and psychological stages of development across the life span.

Identify the full spectrum of sexual expression, including auto-erotic behavior, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, questioning, intersex and asexual (LGBTQQIA+), as well as sex among the disabled, young, and elderly.
Evaluate the biological, social, and psychological issues associated with conception, pregnancy and birth, including reproductive justice.
Evaluate relevant health information, including healthy relationships, sexual dysfunction, sexually transmitted infections, and commercial sex.

rows.title: Demystifying the Middle East
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Examine the diverse identities of people of the Middle East in their geographic, historical, and political context.
Assess power dynamics and challenge stereotypes related to the Middle East.
Apply methods of inquiry from the social sciences and humanities to critique Orientalism and explore alternatives.
Analyze activist, feminist, and aesthetic movements in the Middle East, including their major creative expressions.
Explain the importance of major cultural, artistic, and intellectual contributions from the Middle East and the diaspora.

rows.title: Introduction to Ethnic Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze race as a social construct and the changing definitions of race.

Examine the impact and histories of immigration, colonization, and diaspora in the shaping of ethnic and racial formations in the United States, including Native Americans, African Americans, Asian Americans, and Latinx Americans.
Assess historical roots and contemporary consequences of prejudice, discrimination, and institutional racism.

Describe and evaluate major theories of race and ethnicity, and how the intersections of social class, gender, sexuality, and ability pervade racial and ethnic identity formations in the United States.
Analyze representations in the popular press and other media that influence relations in ethnic and racial groups in American society.
Appraise and create artistic and cultural representations that speak to race and ethnicity in the United States.
Identify and evaluate social movements and/or policy debates for racial justice and equity.

rows.title: Trauma and the Arts: An Interdisciplinary Approach
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate works of art across disciplines as to how they respond to historical traumatic events.
Analyze visual art and public monuments in the context of historical events and cultural memory.
Compare literary works, including personal testimony, in terms of figurative language and themes related to the ongoing effects of trauma.
Identify the function of music and dance in bearing witness, cultural resilience, and sustaining community.
Identify and analyze activist artistic responses to personal and political oppression.

rows.title: Diversity and Social Justice: Ableism
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe and analyze ableism as a system of oppression and privilege.
Assess biases and stereotypes regarding ableism.
Examine individual and collective ways to take action in response to ableism.
Explain the intersectionality of ableism with other distinct forms of social oppression.

rows.title: Diversity and Social Justice: Antisemitism/Anti-Arabism
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe and analyze antisemitism and anti-Arabism as systems of oppression and privilege.
Assess biases and stereotypes regarding antisemitism and anti-Arabism.
Examine individual and collective ways of taking action in response to antisemitism and anti-Arabism.
Explain the intersectionality of distinct forms of antisemitism and anti-Arabism with other distinct forms of social oppression.

rows.title: Elementary Italian
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally using present and past tense syntax at a beginning level in Italian.
Read and write in Italian at a beginning level.
Apply clear Italian pronunciation and intonation when responding to spoken Italian at a beginning level.
Explain elements of Italian culture at a level appropriate for a beginning-level Italian language learner.

rows.title: Continuation of Intermediate Conversational Italian
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate in intermediate-high level spoken conversations in Italian using correct pronunciation, grammar, and syntax.
Apply intermediate-high level skills in listening comprehension.
Explain elements of the history, culture and social trends of the Italian-speaking world.

rows.title: Continuation of Elementary Italian
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Read and write in Italian at a near-elementary level.
Communicate orally with correct syntax using the present perfect and imperfect, and the future indicative tenses at a near-elementary level in Italian.
Apply clear Italian pronunciation and intonation when responding to spoken Italian at an elementary level.
Explain and compare elements of Italian culture and society at a near-elementary level.

rows.title: Elementary Japanese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally in Japanese at a basic beginning level.
Interpret the main ideas and grammatical forms of a written text in Japanese at a basic beginning level.
Apply a cultural understanding of Japanese syllabic writing systems and Kanji at a basic beginning level when composing short communications.
Describe basic elements of Japanese culture in relation to diverse communication practices.

rows.title: Beginning Kanji for Reading and Writing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify simple words and phrases using appropriate kanji characters at the beginning level.
Comprehend reading materials at the beginning level.
Compose paragraphs using appropriate kanji characters at the beginning level.

rows.title: Elementary Japanese Part II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally in Japanese at a basic beginning level.
Interpret the main ideas and grammatical forms of a written text in Japanese at a basic beginning level.
Apply a cultural understanding of Japanese syllabic writing systems and Kanji at a basic beginning level when composing short communications
Describe basic elements of Japanese culture in relation to diverse communication practices.

rows.title: Intermediate Japanese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally at a basic intermediate level in Japanese.
Interpret the main ideas and grammatical forms of a written text in Japanese at a basic intermediate level.
Compose short communications in the Japanese syllabic writing systems and Kanji at a basic intermediate level.
Discuss various aspects of Japanese culture.

rows.title: Continuation of Intermediate Japanese
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Communicate orally at a mid-Intermediate level in Japanese.
Analyze the main ideas and grammatical forms of a written text in Japanese at a mid-intermediate level.
Create written communications in the Japanese syllabic writing systems and Kanji at a mid-intermediate level.
Evaluate elements of Japanese culture in relation to diverse communication practices

rows.title: News Reporting and Writing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the characteristics of a good journalist.
Apply the principles and practices of reporting and writing in the production of a news story.
Evaluate the newsworthiness of a story idea by reviewing varying news stories found in a newspaper.
Interpret the ethics and legal rights of a journalist.

rows.title: News Production and Publication II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify journalistic standards and expectations for a news publication at an advanced beginner level
Describe the editorial and operational structure of a campus news publication at an advanced beginner level
Evaluate whether the campus publication meets the information needs of its audience with an advanced beginner level of understanding
Apply advanced-beginner research and writing skills to develop a portfolio of published works for employment opportunities in the field of journalism

rows.title: Data and Multimedia Journalism
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assemble data, text, and imagery for an infographic
Assess the quality of a data set for use in a journalistic article
Apply the basic principles and practices involved in composing an infographic

rows.title: The Latinx Experience in the United States
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Interpret the demographic diversity represented by the terms Latinx/Hispanic through analysis of Latinx produced theory and knowledge.

Assess the impact of U.S. expansionism in the 19th Century and the integration of Latinx populations in the U.S. Southwest and Puerto Rico, accounting for issues of colonialism, race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethno-centrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, sovereignty, and anti-racism.
Evaluate the intersectionality of race and racism in relation to U.S. government immigration policies and how they impact immigrants from Latin America to the U.S.

Debate the impact of Latinxs on U.S. institutions and society during the Civil Rights and Post Civil Rights eras, specifically reviewing acts of resistance and racial and social justice movements in Latinx communities.

Compare selected aspects of the Latinx experience in the United States related to patterns of assimilation and migrant transnationalism, identifying issues such as multiculturalism and language and education policies.
Critique the Latinx community's cultural contributions to the U.S. and their impact on popular culture and as forms of protest that have encouraged agency and equity.

rows.title: Diego Rivera: Art and Social Change in Latin America
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the political impact of the Mexican Revolution on artists and the development of public art in Mexico.
Evaluate Diego Rivera's political, cultural and artistic influences.
Analyze and consider the roles and meanings of politically-oriented Latinx art in the San Francisco Bay Area.
Assess the impact of modern political revolutions on Latin American culture.
Compare key cultural figures that carry on Diego Rivera's legacy.

rows.title: Individual Study in Latin American and Latino/a Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze a research topic or issue in Latin American and Latino/a Studies.
Present an argument that compares similarities and differences among perspectives in Latin American and Latino/a literature.
Synthesize theories and concepts that explain a chosen topic or issue in Latin American and Latino/a Studies.

rows.title: Latin American Workers in the Americas
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize key commonalities and differences between the U.S. and Latin America in the development of the State and the political economy.
Assess the role of U.S. foreign policy in Latin America and its impact on Latin American workers' lives in the U.S. and Latin America.
Compare the development of labor movements in the U.S. and Latin America.
Analyze the processes of immigration from Latin America to the U.S. and its impact on the labor market.
Examine the problems facing the U.S. labor movement in its ability to address contemporary issues facing Latin American workers in both Latin America and the U.S.
Analyze the impact of class, race, and gender on the lives of Latin American workers in the Americas.

rows.title: California Labor History
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
